info.text: Lesson 07 quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: What is a statement in C++?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A program is a list of statements. Each one is a complete instruction: declare a variable, change a value, print something, or control the flow.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: One complete instruction, usually ending with a semicolon
A comment that explains the code
A file that contains the program

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 3;
x = x + 1;
x = x * 2;
cout << x << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Statements run one after another, from top to bottom: 3, then 4, then 8. If the last two lines were swapped the answer would be 7, so the order matters.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What does a block { ... } do?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A block is a bundle of statements. This is why an if or a loop can run many statements instead of only one: we put them together inside braces.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Groups several statements so they can be treated as one
Turns the statements inside it into comments

questiontext.text: What does a lonely extra semicolon ; mean in C++?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. You may write int n = 5;; and it works: the second semicolon is an empty statement. Be careful though: if (x > 3); has an empty statement as its body, a famous bug.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: An empty statement that does nothing

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so that the program prints 140 (the order of the two updates matters!).

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. First 100 - 30 = 70, then 70 * 2 = 140. If the updates were swapped you would get 100 * 2 - 30 = 170.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int hp = 100;
hp = hp - 30;
hp = hp * 2;
cout << hp << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int hp = 40;
if (hp > 50) {
    cout << "Strong" << endl;
} else {
    cout << "Weak" << endl;
}
cout << "Done" << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The condition hp > 50 is false, so the if block is skipped and the else block runs. After the whole if/else is finished, the program continues with the next statement: Done.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which kind of statement can change the normal top-to-bottom order of execution?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Control-flow statements choose a path (if), repeat (while, for) or jump (break, continue, return). All other statements simply run in sequence.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Sort each keyword by the kind of control flow it creates.

Drag the correct label next to every item.

if  →  [[1]]

else  →  [[1]]

while  →  [[2]]

for  →  [[2]]

break  →  [[3]]

return  →  [[3]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. if and else choose between paths. while and for repeat a block. break and return leave the current loop or function immediately.

The correct answer:

Selection (choose): if, else
Iteration (repeat): while, for
Jump (leave or skip): break, return

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int i = 0;
while (i < 3) {
    cout << "*";
    i++;
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2 and stops when i reaches 3: three stars. They are printed side by side because no endl is inside the loop.

name.text: Q10 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct keywords so the program prints Buy.

main.cpp
int coins = 7;
[[1]] (coins >= 5) {
    cout << "Buy" << endl;
} [[2]] {
    cout << "Save" << endl;
}

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A choice between two paths is written with if ... else. while and for are for repeating.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int coins = 7;
if (coins >= 5) {
    cout << "Buy" << endl;
} else {
    cout << "Save" << endl;
}

questiontext.text:
Match each keyword with its job.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

if  →  [[1]]

else  →  [[2]]

while  →  [[3]]

for  →  [[4]]

break  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five keywords give your program decisions and repetition: the heart of control flow.

The correct answer:

  • if → Runs a block only when a condition is true
  • else → Runs when the if-condition was false
  • while → Repeats a block as long as a condition stays true
  • for → Repeats a block with a counter written in one line
  • break → Leaves the loop immediately

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int a = 1;
{
    int b = 2;
    a = a + b;
}
cout << a << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The inner block can use and change a because a was declared outside it. b only lives inside the braces. After the block, a is 3.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines to compute a damage value. The program must print 15.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. bonus needs attack, and damage needs both. Each line uses what the lines above created: 12, then 3, then 15.

The correct answer:

main.cpp

int bonus = attack / 4;
int damage = attack + bonus;
cout << damage << endl;

questiontext.text: In a flowchart, which shape normally represents a decision such as an if?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Rectangles are for actions, ovals for start and end, and the diamond asks a yes/no question with two ways out. That is exactly what an if does.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int score = 75;
if (score >= 90) cout << "A";
else if (score >= 70) cout << "B";
else cout << "C";
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The checks run from top to bottom and stop at the first true one. 75 is not >= 90, but it is >= 70, so B is printed and the final else is skipped.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Is each line a valid statement? Sort them.

Drag the correct label next to every item.

int a = 3;  →  [[1]]

3 + 4;  →  [[1]]

int = 5;  →  [[2]]

{ int z = 1; }  →  [[1]]

if (true) { }  →  [[1]]

while () { }  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A declaration needs a name, a loop needs a condition, and 3 + 4; is legal (though useless). A block alone is also a valid statement. Each line was tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Valid statement: int a = 3;, 3 + 4;, { int z = 1; }, if (true) { }
Not valid: int = 5;, while () { }

name.text: Q17 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Complete the loop so it adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 and prints 10.

Drag the correct pieces into the gaps.

main.cpp
int total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i [[1]] 4; i[[2]]) {
    total += i;
}
cout << total << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The loop must include 4, so the test is i <= 4. And the counter must grow with i++. With < the last number would be missed and the total would be 6.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    total += i;
}
cout << total << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) break;
    cout << i << " ";
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. break leaves the whole loop immediately. When i becomes 3 the loop ends before printing, so only 1 and 2 were printed.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each type of control flow with what it means.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Sequence  →  [[1]]

Selection  →  [[2]]

Iteration  →  [[3]]

Jump  →  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Every program you will ever write is built from these four ideas.

The correct answer:

  • Sequence → Statements run one after another
  • Selection → Choose a path with if / else
  • Iteration → Repeat statements with a loop
  • Jump → Leave or skip with break, continue or return

dragbox.text: Choose a path with if / else
Leave or skip with break, continue or return

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) continue;
    cout << i << " ";
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one. Even numbers are skipped, so only the odd numbers 1, 3 and 5 are printed.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.
